title_en: Stingy Bosses and Spare Change: The Office Whip-Round
title_zh: 吝啬的老板与零钱：办公室凑份子
summary_zh: 英国广播公司的一篇报道聚焦办公室凑份子现象：同事们为生日、婚礼或离职等场合集体凑钱送礼，但给多少、如何催收常常引发尴尬。受访者大多要求匿名，反映出这一话题的敏感性；资历较浅的员工可能面临更大的经济与社交压力，而高层管理者也可能因频繁的默认期待感到不堪重负。文章还引用了剑桥大学组织心理学教授的建议，主张优先考虑直接同事、避免反复催收，并强调礼物应重象征意义而非金钱价值。
reading_passage:
Office collections for colleagues are a tradition but can raise awkward questions

Love them, hate them or barely know them, it's a colleague's birthday, wedding or leaving do and there's a collection to mark the occasion.

So how much should you give? And if you're the person organising the collection, how do you chase without feeling like a loan shark or exposing unspoken team dynamics?

The politics of the office whip-round are so sensitive that everyone the BBC spoke to asked us not to use their real name.

For those on a tight budget, the rule is simple: only give to colleagues you've worked with directly.

Lucy, a senior therapist in healthcare, says: "If we haven't worked together, my purse is staying shut."

There's a blunter unspoken truth beneath the surface. "It also depends on if I like you," she admits.

"One colleague's whole demeanor annoyed me, so when she moved roles, I wanted to celebrate with my own drink - not give her money."

Former music journalist Layla is similar, only contributing if she "really likes" the person.

Yet she often avoids office collections on principle, not personality, disliking how impersonal they can feel.

"I'd rather buy my own gift for someone I care about. I hate having to be forced to contribute to a joint collection out of some rubbish sense of obligation," she says.

The decision to give also comes with a question of how much.

Barker has a decade's worth of experience organising and contributing to various collections at a large multi-national company, where he works in research and production.

He says it's normally the same half a dozen people that contribute generously, irrespective of the person or the occasion.

The average a worker gave to a collection was £11.65 in the first three months of the year, according to analysis of over 5,000 contributions by website GiftRound.

We ask workers in London how much they'd give towards a colleague's leaving gift

Junior workers can often face the biggest dilemma. Felicity, now mid-career, remembers one horror story from her first job as a teenager.

Working at a car garage aged 17, she was suddenly thrust an envelope to give money for a mechanic who was retiring. The team was small and tight-knit, so everyone was expected to contribute.

"Not only did I not really know anyone at that stage, but I also had no money to give - I was still living at home and being paid hardly anything.

"As it was after lunch, I'd used my notes. In a panic I threw in all the spare change I had left, basically a load of coppers."

She says: "I thought I'd got away with it until the person collecting shouted 'who on earth put in all this change'. Everyone laughed and I couldn't ever admit it was me."

Today, Felicity usually gives between £5 and £10 but goes up to £20 for a close work friend or long-time colleague.

Barker says it tends to be rank-and-file workers who contribute most often.

"Surprisingly – to me – they're not some of the best paid people in the department," he explains. "Often those in senior positions don't give".

Those on big wages not paying their way may seem stingy. But the reality from the top can look very different, as former senior civil service veteran Darren explains.

In a leadership position managing over 200 people, many of them contractors, office collections were common as staff churn was frequent.

The politics of the office whip-round can be a sensitive topic

Darren found the implicit expectation to give as director became overwhelming.

"Eventually I found I just couldn't keep up and would be spending hundreds, often on people I didn't know at all," he says.

As a middle ground, he decided to sign cards and only give money if he'd had direct contact. This stopped him feeling disingenuous and giving resentfully.

But the card-not-cash compromise has become harder as collections move online, with amounts often shown alongside the names of individuals by default.

Of course, these days, alongside emails, there's always the ever-present work WhatsApp group.

Healthcare worker Jeffrey says he's still reeling from seeing staff donations toward the family of a deceased patient being openly listed in the agency chat, individual donation amounts included.

Should you chase contributions - and note who's given and who has not?

"I send one email to those who haven't paid, making clear that those who have contributed are not included in the email. You'd be surprised how quickly people reply," she says.

She then gets a more junior colleague to send another, final, chaser on her behalf.

"And yes, I keep a list on paper, too. I don't forget," she adds.

"I don't like to nag," he says. Instead he prefers a single reminder to all that preserves team unity.

Thomas Roulet, professor of organisational psychology and leadership at Cambridge University, says:

Prioritise direct colleagues and close relationships: It's generally socially acceptable to limit giving toward wider team members

Do not chase people individually: And do not chase them collectively more than once. Some may be financially struggling

Include a card as an alternative: It costs the contributor nothing and feels like a souvenir for the recipient

The gift should be symbolic: Choose a gift for its individual significance rather than monetary value.

vocabulary.example: Asking a colleague for money can create an awkward silence.
She faced a dilemma over whether to report the payroll error.
He felt a strong obligation to attend the retirement lunch.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 缺乏人情味的；不针对个人的
vocabulary.example: Automated messages can make workplace communication feel impersonal.

vocabulary.meaning_zh: 同事间为送礼凑的钱；凑份子
vocabulary.example: They organised a whip-round after the team leader announced her departure.
On a tight budget, he limited his donation to direct colleagues.
He tipped the contents of his pocket onto the desk, revealing only spare change.
I decided to throw in a few euros even though I did not know the retiree well.
She assumed she would get away with forgetting to sign the card.
There was an implicit assumption that all managers would donate generously.

difficult_sentences.sentence: So how much should you give? And if you're the person organising the collection, how do you chase without feeling like a loan shark or exposing unspoken team dynamics?
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 主句是两个并列的疑问句；第二个疑问句包含 if 引导的条件状语从句 `if you're the person organising the collection`，并用 `without + V-ing` 结构 `without feeling... or exposing...` 说明催收可能带来的负面感受，突出问题的社交敏感性。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: 并列疑问句；条件状语从句；without + 动名词
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 那你应该给多少？如果你是组织募捐的人，你该如何催款，而又不让人觉得你像放高利贷者或暴露团队中未言明的微妙关系？

difficult_sentences.sentence: Not only did I not really know anyone at that stage, but I also had no money to give - I was still living at home and being paid hardly anything.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 句首 `Not only` 引起倒装，助动词 did 置于主语 I 之前；`not only...but also...` 连接两重负面信息；破折号后的并列分句补充说明经济状况。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: Not only 句首倒装；not only...but also...；破折号补充说明
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 我不仅在那时几乎不认识任何人，而且也没有钱可给——我仍住在家里，工资极低。

difficult_sentences.sentence: As a middle ground, he decided to sign cards and only give money if he'd had direct contact.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: 介词短语 `As a middle ground` 作状语，主句由 and 连接两个并列动作 `decide to sign cards` 和 `only give money`，`if he'd had direct contact` 为条件状语从句，限定给钱的条件。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: As 短语作状语；并列谓语；条件状语从句
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 作为折中方案，他决定只在卡片上签名，只有与对方有过直接接触时才给钱。

difficult_sentences.sentence: But the card-not-cash compromise has become harder as collections move online, with amounts often shown alongside the names of individuals by default.
difficult_sentences.explanation_zh: `But` 表示转折；主句为 `the card-not-cash compromise has become harder`；`as collections move online` 为时间/原因状语从句；`with amounts often shown...` 是 with 复合结构，其中 `shown alongside the names...` 为过去分词短语作宾语补足语，补充说明在线平台默认公开捐款金额。
difficult_sentences.grammar_point: 转折连词；as 引导状语从句；with 复合结构
difficult_sentences.translation_zh: 但随着募捐转到线上，只签名不给现金的折中做法变得更难了，因为平台默认会显示每个人的捐款金额及姓名。

idioms.meaning_zh: 支付自己应付的费用；自食其力
idioms.usage_note: 常用于否定语境，批评那些受益却不承担应有费用的人；工作场合中可指高收入者不参与集体凑钱。
idioms.example: Managers who never pay their way may be resented even if they earn far more than their team.

idioms.usage_note: 名词短语，常与 find、reach、seek 连用，表示在两种极端做法之间寻找可接受的办法。
idioms.example: Signing the card without giving cash was a middle ground between full participation and opting out.

idioms.usage_note: 非正式且带贬义，暗示咄咄逼人地追讨钱财；在文中用于比喻催收份子钱的人。
idioms.example: Sending repeated payment reminders can make an organiser feel like a loan shark rather than a colleague.

idioms.usage_note: 介词短语作状语，描述因紧张或突发压力而仓促做出的行为，常与 throw、grab、run 等动词搭配。
idioms.example: In a panic, she grabbed the envelope and dropped in whatever coins she had left.

reading_questions.question: What is the main issue discussed in the passage?

options.A: Office collections create awkward social and financial decisions for workers.
options.B: Senior managers are consistently more generous than rank-and-file workers.
options.C: Online donation platforms always display individual contribution amounts.
options.D: Workplace collections should be replaced by personal cards and symbolic gifts.

reading_questions.question: Which three occasions are mentioned as triggers for a workplace collection?

options.C: Leaving dos, anniversaries, and staff churn

reading_questions.question: What can be inferred from the two questions in paragraph 3?

options.A: Organisers are usually perceived as loan sharks by their colleagues.
options.B: Most office workers refuse to contribute to collections.
options.C: Deciding how much to give and how to chase are both delicate social tasks.
options.D: Team dynamics improve once a collection is announced.

reading_questions.question: In paragraph 4, the word "sensitive" is closest in meaning to which of the following?

options.C: Requiring careful handling to avoid embarrassment or conflict

reading_questions.question: What is the author's attitude toward junior workers facing collections?

options.B: Critical of their lack of planning
options.D: Sympathetic, noting they often face the biggest dilemma

reading_questions.question: Which best describes the structure of the passage?

options.A: An introduction, personal cases and data, then expert guidance
options.B: A list of reasons to abolish office collections
options.C: A chronological history of workplace giving in the UK
options.D: A comparison between cash and online collection methods

reading_questions.question: Which title best fits the passage?

options.C: Office Collections: Awkward Questions of Money and Obligation
options.D: How Much to Give at Work: A Guide for Managers

sources.title: Stingy bosses and spare change: How much should you give to the office whip-round?
